_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a2.1: Let it write “You may not eat them”: since above [the passage] already spoke of “your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes,” etc. [Deuteronomy 12:6].
rashi:a3.1: Bread, parched grain and fresh stalks: before the omer.
rashi:a3.2: Parched grain [kali]: that was dried in an oven.
rashi:a3.3: Fresh stalks [karmel]: that was rubbed by hand and not singed in the fire.
rashi:a5.1: Parched grain and fresh stalks are in their unadulterated form, since they are not ground.
rashi:a5.2: Parched grain was increased: in the omer meal offering, as it is written concerning it (Leviticus 2[:14]): “parched with fire.” And although karmel is written in that verse, it was made fit only by means of the fire, as we say in Menaḥot (66b): there was a tube for parched grain there, perforated like a sieve, so that the fire would reach all of it. And the word karmel means rakh u-mal, soft and rubbed: soft, that was rubbed.
rashi:a6.1: Bread is found among meal offerings, since the shewbread is called a meal offering, and [so are] the two loaves of Shavuot, of which it is written (Numbers 28[:26]): “When you bring a new meal offering.”
rashi:a7.1: Since they are in their unadulterated form: therefore you cannot derive it [bread from them], for when we say, “What about parched grain, which is in its unadulterated form?” one cannot say, “Fresh stalks will prove it.”
rashi:a7.2: Since they were increased with regard to meal offerings: and when you refute, “What about parched grain, which was increased by way of meal offerings?” one cannot say, “Bread will prove it.”
rashi:a10.1: Piggul is one of the fundamentals of the Torah: that one is liable to karet for it. And the verse did not teach it to be [punished] with karet; it is stated only in [the portion] Kedoshim Tihyu: “And whoever eats it shall bear his iniquity” [Leviticus 19:8]. And although piggul is written there, it is not speaking of full piggul but of one who intends during slaughter [to eat it] outside its place, for so we expound in Torat Kohanim and in [the chapter] Sheḥitat Kodashim (Zevaḥim 28b): if it is not relevant to [intent] outside its time, apply it to [intent] outside its place. And one cannot say that this karet applies to [intent outside its place], for concerning full piggul it is written in Tzav et Aharon: “And the soul that eats of it shall bear her iniquity” [Leviticus 7:18], and we expound in Torat Kohanim: “of it” shall bear her iniquity, and not of its fellow, that is, [intent] outside its place, of which an intention like it is written.
rashi:a11.1: And it is stated there: concerning notar, in the portion Kedoshim Tihyu: “And whoever eats it shall bear his iniquity,” etc. Just as there, in Kedoshim Tihyu, it is karet, as it is written: “and [that soul] shall be cut off.”
rashi:a11.2: It is stated here: in Tzav et Aharon, concerning full piggul: “And the soul that eats,” etc.; and there it is written, “it shall not be credited,” which is full piggul, [intent] outside its time.
rashi:a12.1: And the verse taught it only: [the verse taught] notar [to be punished] with karet only through a verbal analogy, for we would not know that this karet of Kedoshim Tihyu speaks of notar, since it is written after the verse about [intent] outside its place and seems to refer to it; [we know it] only because of the verbal analogy “sacred” and “sacred.”
rashi:a14.1: One’s daughter from the woman he raped is one of the fundamentals of the Torah: that [the punishment] is by burning.
rashi:a15.1: It is derived from “they” [henna] and “they”: it is written concerning one’s wife (Leviticus 18:17): “The nakedness of a woman and her daughter you shall not uncover,” which implies her daughter from him and her daughter from another man, and the end of that verse is: “they [henna] are near kinswomen; it is lewdness.” And it is written (ibid. [18:10]): “The nakedness of your son’s daughter or of your daughter’s daughter,” and that is written about a woman he raped, since his daughter’s daughter from his wife is already derived from the earlier verse, “the nakedness of a woman and her daughter.” And his daughter [herself] is not written concerning the woman he raped; rather, it is derived from “they” and “they” from his wife. Concerning his wife it is written, “they are near kinswomen; it is lewdness,” and concerning the woman he raped it is written, “for they are your own nakedness.” Just as there his daughter is written, as it is written, “a woman and her daughter,” so too here, concerning the woman he raped, [the verse] made his daughter like his daughter’s daughter. And if you say it is an a fortiori inference: one does not issue a prohibition on the basis of a logical inference.
rashi:a16.1: “Lewdness” and “lewdness” for burning: “If a man takes a woman and her mother, it is lewdness” (Leviticus 20:14).
rashi:a17.1: Those who are stoned: for most of those liable to stoning, such as one who has intercourse with his mother or with his daughter-in-law, stoning is not written, only “their blood shall be upon them” (ibid. [Leviticus 20]).
rashi:a19.1: One who blends: to apply from it, is liable, as it is written (Exodus 30:33): “Whoever compounds any like it.”
rashi:a19.2: And one who applies from it: when he did not blend it [himself].
rashi:a19.3: “Or whoever puts any of it”: of that [oil] of Moses.
rashi:a21.1: In halves: for example, six log, since that of Moses was a hin, twelve log.
rashi:a21.2: Halves of the incense: 184 maneh, since every day he burned a maneh, as we say below (Keritot 6a): 365 maneh, corresponding to the number of days of the solar year.
rashi:a22.1: A portion [peras] in the morning: half a maneh.
rashi:a23.2: Aromatic cinnamon, five hundred: for so the verse says: “half of it, two hundred and fifty.” It said “half of it” for this reason: that they should not weigh it all together but in halves, so that there would be two surpluses there.
rashi:a24.1: This is what was difficult for the tanna: that is, this is why the baraita teaches us [the total], for from the plain sense of the verse I would have said that aromatic calamus is like aromatic cinnamon, that the verse’s “half of it” refers to both of them. [The baraita] teaches us [otherwise].
rashi:a25.1: Half and half: that they would weigh in halves.
rashi:a26.1: Precisely [ayin be’ayin]: so that the spice does not tip [the scale].
rashi:a26.2: [The printed text marks this comment “ע״א”.] The Omnipresent knows the surpluses: that he would not weigh the surpluses by themselves, but leaves them as they are, and the Omnipresent knows what their weight is. [The comment ends with the words “perush Romi.”]
rashi:a27.1: Rather, Rav Yehuda said, this is what was difficult for him, etc. [Rashi’s heading includes “this is what was difficult for him,” which the printed Gemara does not have.] This is the reading: “Rather, Rav Yehuda said.” Since he brings it twice, he certainly does so in order to add [a surplus].
rashi:a28.1: That one should not place a weight, etc.: that he should weigh each and every spice against the iron [weight], and not weigh by the count of the myrrh and then go back and weigh the cassia against the myrrh.
rashi:a29.2: Is not sufficient: since the oil was only twelve log, and the roots were many.
rashi:a29.3: And soaked them in water [Rashi reads “soaked”; the printed text reads “boiled”]: so that they would absorb the water, and when he floated the oil over them they would not absorb it.
rashi:a29.4: And the oil absorbed the fragrance, and he removed it [vekipeḥo]: he wiped it off; its like is “kipaḥta et haro’eh” in Yoma (83b). Moses wiped the oil off the roots and put it in a flask.
rashi:b1.1: And was just one miracle performed with it: [as if to say,] you wonder that it would not suffice? [It sufficed] even to anoint Aaron and his sons all seven days of inauguration, as is explained in the first chapter of Yoma (5a): “Seven days shall he consecrate you” (Leviticus 8:33), and anointing is juxtaposed to consecration, as it is written: “to be anointed in them and to be consecrated in them” (Exodus 29:29).
rashi:b2.1: “This shall be to Me throughout your generations”: evidently all twelve log remain for the future.
rashi:b4.1: Jehoiakim: was older than Jehoahaz by two years, as it is written of [Jehoahaz] (II Kings 23:31): “Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he reigned three months,” and of Jehoiakim it is written (ibid. [23:36]): “He was twenty-five years old when he became king.” So Jehoiakim is found to be older than Jehoahaz by two years. So it is taught in Seder Olam.
rashi:b7.1: At a time when there is peace in Israel: the kingdom is an inheritance and does not require anointing; but when there is a dispute, it is not an inheritance, and it requires anointing at the outset.
rashi:b8.1: But not the kings of Israel: from when David came; but Saul was anointed.
rashi:b10.1: And due to the dispute with Joram he was anointed, etc.: granted, a king son of a king of the house of David: when there is a dispute, we derive from the verses that he returns to the original rule of anointing. But the kings of Israel are not fit for anointing at all.
rashi:b10.2: With pure balsam: he was anointed, and not with the anointing oil.
rashi:b11.1: This is the reading: [And Rabbi] Yoḥanan said: He is Jehoahaz; Zedekiah is Shallum.
rashi:b13.1: But it counts them in a row: since it counts third and fourth.
rashi:b13.2: Because Jeconiah reigned: the son of Jehoiakim, in place of Jehoiakim his father, before Zedekiah.
rashi:b17.1: As it is stated, “And the vessels of gold,” etc.: since it is written “in a coffer by its side,” evidently wherever the Ark was, the coffer was with it, and when [the Ark] was sequestered, it was sequestered with it.
rashi:b17.2: Put the Ark: in the house that Solomon built; it shall no longer be a burden on your shoulders [II Chronicles 35:3]. And we read in Tractate Shekalim (6:1): He said to them: If it goes into exile with you to Babylonia, you will no longer bring it back on your shoulders; and he sequestered it.
rashi:b18.1: The jar: derived from “there” and “there.” It is written concerning the Ark (Exodus 30:6): “Where I will meet with you there,” and concerning the jar it is written (ibid. 16[:33]): “And put there an omer-full of manna.”
rashi:b19.1: And the anointing oil: derived from “generations” and “generations,” from the jar.
rashi:b20.1: Aaron’s staff: derived from “to be kept” and “to be kept,” from the jar. It is written of the staff (Numbers 17:25): “to be kept for a sign against the rebellious children,” and of the jar: “to be kept throughout your generations.”
rashi:b21.1: Like a crown: around his head.
rashi:b21.2: Like a chi: a Greek letter, made like this: X. For he pours oil on his head and afterward [puts oil] between his eyelashes, and joins them with his finger by way of the forehead.
rashi:b24.1: Mesaper: speaks. Another version: mistaper, has his hair cut, when he cuts his hair.
rashi:b24.2: Perhaps I misused: by putting too much there.
rashi:b26.1: And I misused: since my garments benefit from the fragrance of the oil in my beard.
rashi:b27.1: Gihon: a small spring near Jerusalem, and not the great Gihon that goes out of Eden.
rashi:b29.1: Should raise a hen [Rashi reads tarnegolta, a hen; the printed text reads tarnegola, a rooster]: for this purpose.
rashi:b30.1: In a dark house [beveita debahata]: somewhat dark.
tosafot:a2.1: If so, let the verse write “You may not eat them”: and [the Gemara] could not say [the extra wording is] because it should have said only “your grain,” [and then derived wine and oil from it, so that the full list shows] one [is flogged] for each one separately. For there is a refutation: grain was increased with regard to ḥalla, wine with libations, and oil with meal offerings; and grain cannot be derived from wine and oil, since they have an aspect of increase with regard to the altar. But it is difficult: let it write grain and oil, or grain and wine, and derive the remaining one from them.
tosafot:a9.1: But say that for parched grain, which is superfluous, one is liable once, etc.: above, concerning the fat of an ox, a sheep and a goat, [the Gemara] could have raised the same challenge.
tosafot:b8.1: The kings of Israel are not anointed: from David onward, since concerning him a limitation is written: “this one” requires anointing and not another. But Saul, who was before that, was anointed.
tosafot:b12.1: He filled the place of his fathers: and although he was wicked, perhaps at that time he was righteous.
gershom:a1.1: [Editor’s note: up to here belongs to 4b.] And still: why is he flogged? It is a general prohibition, and [the verse is] not for dividing [the prohibitions].
gershom:a2.1: If so: that it is merely for the sake of a general prohibition, let the verse say “You may not eat them,” since it already mentioned them.
gershom:a3.1: Bread, parched grain and fresh stalks: before the omer.
gershom:a4.1: That parched grain is in its unadulterated form: that it was not ground and not mixed with water and salt.
gershom:a5.1: That parched grain was increased with regard to meal offerings: “Ears of grain parched with fire, groats of karmel” [Leviticus 2:14]. This karmel is rakh u-mal, soft and rubbed, as the Targum renders it: perukhan rekhikhan, soft groats.
gershom:a6.1: Fresh stalks were not increased with regard to meal offerings, since this karmel of “you shall not eat” is completely dry, as the Targum renders: “bread and parched grain and perukhan,” and does not write rekhikhan [soft] of it.
gershom:a7.1: What about fresh stalks, which have not changed from their original state: at all, for it was not roasted and not ground.
gershom:a8.1: What about parched grain and fresh stalks: since they are in their unadulterated form, for they were not ground and not mixed with water and salt.
gershom:a9.1: Rabbi Yitzḥak could say to you: parched grain is superfluous, [so that the verse] need not write parched grain. And if you refute: [what about] fresh stalks, which have not changed from their original state, even by roasting? Bread will prove it.
gershom:a10.1: Therefore parched grain is superfluous: to obligate lashes. Why did it write parched grain in the middle, between bread and fresh stalks? This is what it is saying: bread, like parched grain, he is liable; fresh stalks, like parched grain, he is liable: to obligate [lashes] for each one.
gershom:a11.1: For piggul, one who intends to eat it outside its time, is one of the fundamentals of the Torah, and the verse taught it [to be punished] with karet only by a verbal analogy, for he derives “iniquity” and “iniquity” from notar. It is stated here, concerning notar: “And whoever eats it shall bear his iniquity”; and this piggul here is [intent] outside its place, for “it shall not be credited” is written of it here. And it is stated there concerning piggul: “shall bear her iniquity.” Just as there, concerning notar, it is karet, as it is written, “And whoever eats it,” etc., “and [that soul] shall be cut off,” etc., so too here it is karet.
gershom:a12.1: For notar: the verse taught it only by a verbal analogy, for he derives “sacred” and “sacred.” Here it is written: “because he has profaned the sacred thing of the Lord,” and there it is written: “You shall burn the leftovers in fire; it shall not be eaten, for it is sacred.” Just as there it is notar, so too here it is notar and not piggul, even though piggul is written in it, for that is [intent] outside its place, in keeping with its position [in the passage].
gershom:a13.1: For one’s daughter from the woman he raped: [the verse] taught it only by a verbal analogy, as Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Avdimi said: it is derived from “they” and “they” for the prohibition. It is written here, concerning the prohibition: “The nakedness of a woman and her daughter you shall not uncover; you shall not take her son’s daughter or her daughter’s daughter,” etc. And this that it says, “the nakedness of a woman and her daughter,” speaks of a woman with whom he has marriage, whether her daughter whom she had from another man or her daughter whom she has from him. And it is written: “The nakedness of your son’s daughter or of your daughter’s daughter, you shall not uncover their nakedness, for they are your own nakedness”; and here “woman” is not written, which implies that all these do not speak of marriage but of rape. We have found his son’s daughter and his daughter’s daughter from the woman he raped; from where do we know his daughter from the woman he raped? And if you say an a fortiori inference: one does not punish on the basis of a logical inference. Rather, it is derived from “they” and “they” for the prohibition: just as here, concerning “the nakedness of a woman and her daughter,” [the verse] revealed [the law of] his daughter from marriage, so too here, concerning “the nakedness of your son’s daughter or your daughter’s daughter,” he is also liable for his daughter from the woman he raped. And it is derived from “lewdness” and “lewdness” for burning: it is written here, concerning “the nakedness of a woman and her daughter,” “lewdness,” and we have already derived his daughter from the woman he raped from it as well, since it is written of it too [Editor’s note: it appears it should read: since “for they are your own nakedness” is also written of it, and we derive “they” and “they” from there, so it is as though “lewdness” were also written of it; and it is written regarding burning, etc.] (“they are near kinswomen; it is lewdness”). And it is written regarding burning, “lewdness,” as it is written: “And if a man takes a woman and her mother, it is lewdness.” Just as this is by burning, so too this is by burning, and his daughter from the woman he raped as well.
gershom:a14.1: Just as a necromancer and a sorcerer are by stoning, as it is written: “They shall stone them with stones; their blood shall be upon them.”
gershom:a15.1: One who blends: in order to apply from it, is liable; [that is, he] does not hand it over to the community, and he transgresses “Upon the flesh of a person it shall not be poured” and “according to its composition,” etc. And likewise one who applies from it, who did not make it, is exempt, even though the other handed it over to the community. What is the reason? Because one is liable only, etc.
gershom:a16.1: Just as with the oil, when he blends it in halves he is exempt, as is explained further on.
gershom:a17.1: “That you shall make”: is written [meaning] every making of incense; that is, that whole measure that is burned, it is forbidden to blend like it. And it is possible to burn the incense in halves, a portion in the morning and a portion in the afternoon, since one maneh was burned each day. Therefore, when he blends it in halves he is liable.
gershom:a18.1: Also aromatic calamus, half of it two hundred and fifty: that is, that all of it is five hundred, and they would come to two thousand.
gershom:a19.1: But say that it is indeed so: let us say two thousand.
gershom:a20.1: If so, let the verse say for both, for aromatic cinnamon and for aromatic calamus: half of it, two hundred and fifty. Since it does not say “half of it” for calamus, conclude from it that it is one thousand seven hundred and fifty.
gershom:a21.1: The Merciful One writes “a like weight” [bad bevad]: weight against weight, that is, precisely.
gershom:a22.1: And you say with a surplus: that is, that he would afterward weigh the surpluses by themselves to know how much surplus there is in them. But since it is written “a like weight,” evidently there is no surplus in them.
gershom:a23.1: But doesn’t Rav Yehuda say: The Omnipresent knows the surpluses [Rabbeinu Gershom, like the Aramaic of the daf, reads Rav Yehuda; the English translation has Rabbi Yehuda]: that is, he would not weigh the surpluses by themselves, but leaves them as they are, and the Omnipresent knows what their weight is. Evidently he holds that there is a surplus for every shekel.
gershom:a24.1: Abaye could say to you [in Rabbeinu Gershom’s version this answer is Abaye’s]: Rav Yehuda, who holds there is a surplus, derives it from here, for he holds: aromatic cinnamon, why do they bring it in halves, in two times? Rather, conclude from it that there is a surplus in them, and the Omnipresent knows how many surpluses, and there is no fixed measure for the surplus.
gershom:a25.1: And what is “a like weight” that it says? Not that it means precisely, but that one should not place a weight [together with] a weight and weigh. That is, he should not place the stone weight of two hundred and fifty with the [other] two hundred and fifty and weigh a shekel-weight of five hundred that way; rather, for each weight he should place its own stone. That is “a like weight.”
gershom:a26.1: Another version: from which it follows that there is a surplus in it, as R. Yehuda said: aromatic cinnamon, why do they bring half of it, of five hundred, two hundred [and fifty], etc. [Editor’s note: that is, the other version does not read “Rather, Rav Yehuda could say to you,” but only “as Rav Yehuda said,” etc., and Rav Yehuda himself brought proof from the verse. It appears that this is why Rashi wrote “this is the reading: Rather, Rav Yehuda said,” etc., meaning to exclude the reading of the other version.]
gershom:a27.1: The anointing oil that Moses made in the wilderness: as it is written, “And of olive oil a hin” [Exodus 30:24]; in it they cooked the roots, the myrrh, etc., so that they would absorb the fragrance.
gershom:a28.1: Rather, he brought the roots and they soaked them in water so that they would not absorb any of the oil. And he would throw the water out and pour the oil over the roots, and he floated oil over them so that they would be covered, and the oil absorbed the fragrance from the spices.
gershom:a29.1: And removed it [vekipeḥo]: he would remove it at once, so that the roots would not absorb the oil.
gershom:a30.1: Rabbi Yehuda said to him: What need is there for this? And was just one miracle, etc. [An editor’s note here marks the end of the material that belongs to 5a.]
gershom:b1.1: The kingdom is an inheritance, and it does not require anointing.
gershom:b2.1: And not whenever the king wishes does he bequeath the kingdom to his sons without anointing.
gershom:b3.1: “In the midst of Israel”: at a time when he dwells in the midst of Israel in peace, when there is no dispute among them, he bequeaths the kingdom to his sons.
gershom:b4.1: Let him derive it from the fact that he was the first king: since he was not the son of a king.
gershom:b5.1: As Rav Pappa says below: they anointed him with pure balsam, since Jehoiakim was older than him by two years.
gershom:b6.1: Rather, Jehoahaz was older, since it calls him firstborn.
gershom:b7.1: No, it calls him firstborn for this reason: that he is firstborn to the kingship, since he reigned before his brother.
gershom:b8.1: But it counts them in a row: that is, third and then fourth; for he is fourth to the kingship.
gershom:b9.1: Because Jeconiah [the text calls him “ben dodo”] reigned before him, and he went into exile, and his exiles with him, before the destruction; and in the end Zedekiah reigned.
gershom:b10.1: And was there anointing oil in the days of Jehoahaz? But it was sequestered in the days of Josiah his father, as it is taught: From when the Ark was sequestered, etc.
gershom:b11.1: “You shall put in a coffer by its side”: that is, that it was sequestered by the side of the Ark.
gershom:b12.1: And Rabbi Elazar said: the jar of manna that was sequestered is derived from “there” and “there.” Here it is written, “And put there an omer-full of manna,” and concerning the Ark it is written, “And I will meet with you there.” And concerning the jar, “to be kept” is written, and concerning Aaron’s staff: “to be kept for a sign against the rebellious children.”
gershom:b13.1: And it is derived from “generations” and “generations”: concerning the jar it is written, “to be kept throughout your generations,” and concerning the anointing oil: “This shall be to Me throughout your generations.” This teaches that all of them were sequestered.
gershom:b14.1: Like a crown: they anointed him on his forehead from ear to ear and at the back of his neck behind him, that is, all around. Like a Greek chi [the printed text shows the Hebrew letter ח here]: thus, from the forehead over the head to the back of the neck. [Editor’s note: see what is written in Arukh HaShalem, entry “ki” 1, which explains “like a chi.”]
gershom:b15.1: It is taught in one [baraita], etc. The one who says that he first anoints between his eyelashes holds that anointing is preferable, since it was increased with regard to the service vessels, for we do not find pouring with them, only anointing.
gershom:b16.1: Because of “and he anointed him to sanctify him”: already.
gershom:b17.1: When he would speak [mesaper]: they would rise and sit for him on the roots of his beard, so that they would not fall to the ground when he moved his mouth to speak.
gershom:b18.1: And concerning this matter Moses was worried, for Moses would say: perhaps I misused, since [the oil] was not commanded for anointing the beard, and he would see on it two drops that had gone down from the head to the beard.
gershom:b19.1: A Divine Voice emerged, etc. [Aaron said:] Perhaps I misused, since I benefit from the fragrance that is in my beard. A Divine Voice emerged, etc.
gershom:b20.1: If its light continues: until all the oil in the vessel is used up.
gershom:b21.1: Should raise a hen [Rabbeinu Gershom reads tarnegolta, a hen]: in the name of that venture.
